story.storyText:
Mina began her school work experience at Riverside Voice on a hot Monday in August. The community radio station occupied two rooms on top of a grocery store. The machines were old, and the audience was small but loyal. Ms Lee, the station leader, gave Mina a desk by the news window.

That afternoon, an envelope appeared at the studio door. It contained copies of bills for the new town flood warning system. A short note asked the station to look into money spent on river sensors. The author had not written a name.

Mina took time to size up the situation, and then she showed the papers to Ms Lee. The bills carried the same company name, but the addresses were not the same. Three bills referred to sensors that did not appear on the town map. She placed the envelope on Ms Lee's desk.

Ms Lee asked Mina to figure out whether the copies matched public records. They opened the town website and compared dates, prices, and project numbers. The records could not account for nearly a quarter of the repair budget. The missing money was too large to forget.

The annual meeting about flood safety was five days away. Mina and Ms Lee narrowed down the key questions they needed to answer. Were the sensors missing, broken, or listed with a new name? They agreed to seek facts and make a claim only after careful checks.


Mina spent Tuesday at homes by the river. She sounded out local families about the warning system without mentioning the envelope. Some families said the river alarm had remained silent during heavy rain in June. Some had never heard the alarm tested.

In the interviews, Mina set down exact times and places in her notebook. She asked the same basic questions and did not lead them to an answer. An old fisherman called Mr Choi remembered a company team removing two sensors after a storm. He had not seen the sensors return.

Back at the station, Mina lined up the town map with an image from the repair report. The river marks matched, but three sensor symbols had moved. One symbol now sat in the center of a car lot. Weather could not explain the change.

Ms Lee reminded her to base the report on records and things they saw. They walked the river path and took a picture of the sensors they found. Careful questions brought out an honest side of a guard at the water plant. He recalled a truck taking damaged machines to a private yard.

Late that evening, a former project member came forward with a box of work logs. Her name was Aisha Rahman, and she had kept copies after leaving the company. The logs showed that new sensors had been ordered but had never reached the river. She agreed to speak on the radio if the station protected her address.


On Wednesday morning, the flood system company called Riverside Voice. The director said the station was creating fear from a small mistake in the records. He tried to play down the silent alarms and offered to buy a month of advertising. Ms Lee refused to discuss money while a report was being prepared.

Mina wanted to shout, but she held back and kept her voice calm. She asked for the place and test record of the missing sensors. The director promised an email, but the message did not arrive. His answer made the open questions more serious.

The grocery store owner worried that the report might upset the town board. Ms Lee had to deal with demands from the owner, the company, and two board members. She explained that the station would correct a mistake but would not hide facts. Mina watched her remain calm through the calls.

A large sponsor then ended support for the station. The autumn schedule could fall through without the money. Ms Lee told Mina that she could stop the report without blame. Mina chose to continue, and the rest of the team chose to stick by her.

During the evening program, Mr Choi spoke out about the silent river alarm. He described carrying his neighbor to high ground during the June rain. He said that the town must not stand by and must act now. Calls began arriving from families along the river.


Rain returned on Thursday and grew hard through the afternoon. Ms Lee mapped out an emergency broadcast with frequent weather reports. Mina prepared phone numbers for the fire station, hospital, and town office. Joon, the sound expert, tested an extra power machine.

At seven, water entered the station stairway and damaged a cable. Joon worked to sort out the sound problem while Mina moved records to a high shelf. The main radio machine lost power for some minutes. A small battery radio still reached homes by the river.

The town warning system remained silent as the river crossed the red mark. Ms Lee chose to push ahead with the emergency program. Mina read street names slowly and repeated the safe routes. Her clear voice helped get across the need to leave low homes at once.

Aisha called with news from the company yard. Two working sensors were waiting there, still packed in the original boxes. That fact helped clear up the mystery of the false repair reports. The company had charged money for work that had never happened.

The town sent buses while Riverside Voice continued the station signal. Fire crews moved families to the school on the hill. By midnight, the rain became light and the river stopped rising. The small station had helped many families reach safety.


The town board held a public hearing on Friday morning. Aisha sent in copies of the work logs to an officer not connected to the company. Mina showed pictures, bills, and the map without adding guesses. The company director sat across the room with a legal expert.

The officer asked the director to explain the missing repair money. He blamed a computer mistake and a former company member. Aisha then explained the order system and showed her original emails. A company leader also confirmed her report.

The hearing chair asked the two sides to draw up a list of facts they accepted. The list confirmed missing sensors, false work dates, and alarms without tests. It also showed that remaining project money could carry over into immediate repairs. The town board voted to replace the company.

At the end of the hearing, the chair summed up the facts for the public. She stated that the review would continue and that the legal result was still open. Her careful language separated known facts from possible crimes. Mina wrote the full statement in her notebook.

After the hearing, local families and town officers met to iron out a temporary warning plan. Riverside Voice would test a public signal on Fridays until the new sensors worked. The fire station would check homes without radios. Aisha agreed to advise the new project team.


Riverside Voice had lost a sponsor, but new support arrived from local families. Small regular gifts allowed the station to bounce back without accepting company control. The grocery store owner offered the rooms at a lower cost. Ms Lee added a clear rule for future advertising.

Mina used her notes to write up the report for the school newspaper. She described the checks for the facts and the questions that remained open. Aisha read the article to protect private details. Mr Choi checked the times in his interview.

The report rooted out a false money plan. It also led the town to test the emergency systems and publish the results. Students formed a school group to help old neighbors use weather radios. The river community became better prepared for a future storm.

On her final day, Mina recorded a short program about the lessons she had learned. Good reporting, she said, was based on time, facts, and respect for a source. A bold claim could attract an audience, but a careful fact could protect a life. Ms Lee listened from the control room.

When the red studio light became bright, Mina felt that she belonged. She gave the weather report, checked the river level, and introduced the evening music. Her voice traveled from the rooms on top of the grocery store into homes across Riverside. The last broadcast of her school job became the opening broadcast of her new Friday program.
